decks.title: India and its Neighbours — Part 1: Starting Points, Pakistan and China before 1978
goals: Explain why India, Pakistan and China are compared and how similar their starting points were
Describe the stages of Pakistan's development strategy and why its growth was uneven
Describe China's path from 1949 to 1978: the first plan, the Great Leap Forward, communes and the Cultural Revolution

slides.heading: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **why compare**, **similar starting points**, **Pakistan's path** and **China before 1978**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why compare neighbours, similar starting points, Pakistan's path and China before 1978
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Three large neighbours began their journeys at almost the same time, as poor and mainly agricultural countries. Yet their paths and results turned out quite different. In this part we look at where they started, how Pakistan built its economy, and what China tried before its famous reforms. Comparing neighbours helps us see what India did well and what it can still learn.

slides.heading: Why compare with neighbours?
bullets: Neighbours share **history, geography and similar problems**, so the comparison is fair.
Comparison shows our **strengths and weaknesses** more clearly than looking at India alone.
Countries also group together for trade and cooperation, for example **SAARC (1985)** in South Asia.
slides.narration: Why study the neighbours at all? Because a fair comparison needs countries that faced similar problems. India, Pakistan and China share long borders, a colonial or semi-colonial past, huge populations and poor starting conditions. When we place them side by side, it becomes easier to judge which policies worked. Countries in the region also cooperate, for example through SAARC, set up in 1985.

slides.heading: Similar starting points

visual.alt: Table comparing the three neighbours: India and Pakistan became independent in 1947 and China became the People's Republic in 1949; first plans announced in 1951, 1956 and 1953; all poor and mainly agricultural around 1950; major reforms began in 1991, 1988 and 1978
visual.caption: Similar starting points, different paths.

slides.narration: Look at the first rows of this table. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, and the People's Republic of China was set up in 1949. All three announced five-year plans within a few years: India in 1951, China in 1953 and Pakistan in 1956. Around 1950 all three were poor and depended mainly on farming. The last row shows that each later turned to major reforms, in a different year.

visual.caption: GLF = Great Leap Forward; CR = Cultural Revolution; PRC = People's Republic of China.

slides.narration: This timeline puts the three countries in three lanes. Notice that China moved first and fastest in changing course, with reforms in 1978. Pakistan followed in 1988 and India in 1991. Before that, China went through two very different experiments, the Great Leap Forward of 1958 and the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976. Keep this picture in mind; examiners often test the order of events.

slides.heading: Pakistan: a mixed economy
slides.body_md: Like India, Pakistan gave roles to both the **public** and **private** sectors and followed **import substitution**.

visual.alt: Flow of Pakistan's strategy: mixed economy after 1947, import substitution behind tariffs in the late 1950s and 1960s, the Green Revolution, nationalisation of capital goods industries in the 1970s, a shift to the private sector, and reforms from 1988
visual.caption: Pakistan's path in six steps

slides.narration: Pakistan chose a mixed economy, much like India. In the late 1950s and 1960s it built consumer goods industries behind high tariffs, which is import substitution. In the 1960s the Green Revolution raised grain output. In the 1970s it nationalised capital goods industries. Then, from the late 1970s, it turned back towards the private sector, and in 1988 it began economic reforms.

slides.heading: Green Revolution and the 1970s in Pakistan
bullets: High-yielding seeds raised **food-grain output**, especially wheat.
Farming became more **mechanised**; the state invested in **infrastructure** in some regions.
1970s: **capital goods industries nationalised**.
Late 1970s and 1980s: **denationalisation**; encouragement to private firms.
slides.narration: The Green Revolution changed farming in Pakistan as it did in India. New seeds, fertilisers and irrigation raised the output of food grains. It also brought machines to farms and more public spending on roads and canals in some regions. In industry, the 1970s saw nationalisation of capital goods industries. Later the direction reversed, and private firms were encouraged again.

slides.heading: Reforms of 1988 and sources of foreign exchange
slides.body_md: Pakistan began **reforms in 1988**. For much of its history, foreign exchange came largely from **outside support**.

rows: Remittances from workers abroad (many in West Asia)
Depend on jobs in other countries
Loans and aid from other countries
Depend on donors' decisions and conditions
Exports of mainly primary and simple goods

visual.alt: Table of Pakistan's main sources of foreign exchange and why each is uncertain: remittances depend on jobs abroad, loans and aid on donors, and exports of simple goods on swinging prices

slides.narration: Facing a financial crisis, Pakistan began economic reforms in 1988. Its foreign exchange came from three main places, shown here. Workers abroad, many of them in West Asia, sent money home. Other countries gave loans and aid. Exports grew, but they were mostly simple, lower value goods. Look at the second column: each source depends on something outside the country's control.

slides.heading: Quick check: Pakistan in the 1970s
slides.body_md: True or false? In the 1970s Pakistan privatised all its capital goods industries.
slides.narration: Think carefully about the direction of policy in the 1970s. Was it towards the state or towards private owners?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: comparing per capita growth
slides.body_md: Two imagined countries. Which one raises living standards faster?
bullets: Step 1 — Per capita income growth is roughly **GDP growth minus population growth**.
Step 2 — Country P: 6 − 2.5 = **3.5 per cent**.
Step 3 — Country Q: 5 − 1 = **4 per cent**.
Step 4 — Q improves average incomes faster, even though its GDP grows more slowly.

visual.alt: Table of two imagined countries: P grows at 6 per cent with population growth 2.5, so per capita income grows about 3.5 per cent; Q grows at 5 per cent with population growth 1, so per capita income grows about 4 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined figures: the slower-growing economy improves living standards faster.

slides.narration: Here is a skill you will use throughout this chapter. Country P has faster GDP growth, but its population also grows fast. Subtract population growth from GDP growth to estimate how fast income per person rises. P gets about three and a half per cent, while Q gets about four per cent. So the slower growing economy is actually improving average living standards faster.

slides.heading: Why Pakistan's growth was uneven

visual.alt: Flow of causes of uneven growth in Pakistan: weather-dependent farm output, remittances and aid from abroad, a narrow export base and political instability
visual.caption: Why growth was hard to sustain

slides.narration: Economists usually give four reasons why Pakistan found it hard to keep growth steady. Farm output depended on the weather. Foreign exchange depended on remittances and aid. The export base stayed narrow. And frequent political changes made long term planning difficult. When several of these went wrong in the same year, growth fell sharply. A strong base of manufactured exports could have cushioned these shocks.

slides.narration: Remember the three reform years and match the right one to Pakistan.

slides.heading: China after 1949
slides.body_md: The People's Republic of China was set up in **1949**. The state directed the economy and launched its **first plan in 1953**.

visual.alt: Flow of China's path before reform: People's Republic 1949, first plan 1953, Great Leap Forward and communes 1958, Cultural Revolution 1966 to 1976, and reforms from 1978
visual.caption: China before 1978

slides.narration: Now let us turn to China. After the People's Republic was set up in 1949, all important sectors were brought under state direction, and the first five year plan began in 1953. Over the next twenty five years China tried two bold campaigns, shown in the middle of this flow, before it changed direction completely in 1978.

slides.heading: The Great Leap Forward (1958)
bullets: Aim: **industrialise the country on a massive scale**, very quickly.
People were encouraged to set up **industries in their backyards**, such as small furnaces for steel.
In rural areas, **communes** were formed to farm land collectively.
slides.narration: In 1958 China launched the Great Leap Forward. The idea was to industrialise at great speed. Villagers were urged to start small industries in their own backyards, including furnaces to make steel. At the same time, rural families were organised into communes, where people farmed the land together. The campaign was meant to pool the country's labour for a giant push.

slides.heading: How a commune worked

rows: Teams of villagers farming land collectively
By the collective, according to work done
Pool labour and land for faster growth
Little extra reward for extra effort

visual.alt: Table of the commune system: villagers farmed land collectively in teams, output was shared by the collective, the aim was to pool labour and land, and the weakness was little extra reward for extra effort

slides.narration: In a commune, teams of villagers farmed the land collectively, and the harvest was shared out by the collective according to work done. The aim was to pool land and labour. But look at the last row. If a family worked harder, its share hardly grew, so there was little extra reward for extra effort. This weakness matters when we study the reforms in Part 2.

slides.heading: Quick check: backyard industries
slides.body_md: What was the intention behind backyard industries during the Great Leap Forward?
slides.narration: Link the backyard furnaces to the main aim of the campaign.

slides.heading: Setbacks and the Cultural Revolution

nodes.label: Severe famine and the withdrawal of Soviet experts
Cultural Revolution (1966–76): students and professionals sent to the countryside

visual.alt: Flow: the Great Leap Forward of 1958 aimed at mass industrialisation, met a severe famine and the withdrawal of Soviet experts, then the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976, and finally reforms from 1978
visual.caption: Setbacks before reform

slides.narration: The Great Leap Forward ran into serious trouble. A severe famine, linked both to drought and to the campaign's own policies, cost a very large number of lives, and a conflict with the Soviet Union led to the withdrawal of its experts. Later, from 1966 to 1976, came the Cultural Revolution, when students and professionals were sent to work and learn in the countryside.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: putting events in order
slides.body_md: Place six events in time, with the country for each.
bullets: Step 1 — Fix the anchors: **1947 and 1949** (new nations).
Step 2 — Plans: **1951** India, **1953** China, **1956** Pakistan.
Step 3 — China's campaigns: **1958**, then **1966–76**.

visual.alt: Table placing events in order with country and year: China first plan 1953, Pakistan first plan 1956, Great Leap Forward 1958, Cultural Revolution 1966 to 1976, Pakistan nationalisation in the 1970s, reforms in China 1978, Pakistan 1988 and India 1991
visual.caption: Tip: memorise the three reform years as 78, 88, 91.

slides.narration: Ordering questions are common in this chapter, so build a simple method. First fix the anchors, 1947 and 1949. Next place the three first plans. Then add China's two campaigns. Finally add the three reform years, which many students remember as seventy eight, eighty eight and ninety one. Write the country next to every date so you never mix them up.

slides.body_md: Arrange the stages of China's development path in the order in which they happened.
slides.narration: Use the anchors from the worked example: founding, first plan, the two campaigns, and then reform.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Mixed economy; import substitution; Green Revolution; nationalisation in the 1970s
State-directed; Great Leap Forward; communes; Cultural Revolution
Mixed economy; five-year plans from 1951; import substitution

visual.alt: Summary table: Pakistan followed a mixed economy, import substitution, the Green Revolution and nationalisation, with reforms from 1988; China was state-directed with the Great Leap Forward, communes and the Cultural Revolution, with reforms from 1978; India followed a mixed economy and plans, with reforms from 1991

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. All three countries began poor and agricultural around 1950 and turned to planning. Pakistan followed a mixed economy, import substitution and the Green Revolution, nationalised in the 1970s and reformed in 1988. China was state directed, tried the Great Leap Forward and communes, went through the Cultural Revolution, and reformed in 1978. India reformed in 1991.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Always write the **country with each date**; mixing up 1978, 1988 and 1991 is the most common slip.
Pakistan **nationalised** in the 1970s; the turn to the private sector came **after** that.
For "why was Pakistan's growth uneven", give **separate** reasons: weather, remittances and aid, narrow exports, instability.
Describe the Great Leap Forward by its **aim** (rapid industrialisation) and its **tools** (backyard industries, communes).
3 marks = three distinct points of about 20 words each; 5 marks = five numbered points.
slides.narration: A few tips before you move on. Always pair a date with its country. Remember that Pakistan nationalised in the 1970s and only later moved towards private firms. When asked for reasons, give separate points rather than one long sentence. And describe the Great Leap Forward by both its aim and its tools. Marks are awarded point by point, so number your points.

decks.title: India and its Neighbours — Part 2: China's Reforms and the Comparison
goals: Explain China's reforms from 1978: household plots, dual pricing, competition and special economic zones
Compare the three countries on population, sectoral composition and human development, using broad patterns
Appraise the development strategies and structure a comparison answer

slides.heading: China's reforms and the three-way comparison

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: China's reforms from 1978, population, output and sectors, human development, and an appraisal
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we see how China changed course in 1978 and why its economy then grew so quickly. After that we compare all three countries on population, on the structure of output, and on human development. We finish by weighing the strengths and limits of each path, and by learning how to write a clear comparison answer.

slides.heading: Reforms from 1978, in phases

rows: Commune land divided into household plots; families kept income after fixed taxes
Private firms and township and village enterprises compete with state-owned enterprises
Dual pricing: fixed price for a quota, market price for the rest
Special economic zones to attract foreign direct investment

visual.alt: Table of China's reforms after 1978: household plots in agriculture first, competition for state-owned enterprises in industry later, dual pricing, and special economic zones for foreign investment

slides.narration: China introduced its reforms step by step. The first phase covered agriculture, foreign trade and investment. In agriculture, commune land was divided among households. In the later phase came industry, where private firms and township and village enterprises were allowed to compete with state owned enterprises. Dual pricing and special economic zones completed the package.

slides.heading: From communes to household plots

rows: Kept by the family after fixed taxes

visual.alt: Table comparing the commune with the household plot: the collective decides versus the family, reward shared by all versus kept by the family after taxes, weak versus strong reason to improve the land

slides.narration: Compare the two columns. In a commune, extra effort was shared by everyone. Under the new system, each family farmed its own plot, paid the taxes fixed by the government, and kept the rest. Suddenly hard work and care for the land paid off for the family itself. This change in incentives is the key to the rise in farm output that followed.

slides.heading: Dual pricing
bullets: Farmers and firms sold a **fixed quota** to the state at **fixed prices**.
Anything produced **above the quota** could be sold at **market prices**.
As output grew, a larger share of goods was traded in markets.
slides.narration: Dual pricing was a clever bridge between the old system and the market. A farmer or factory still had to sell a quota to the state at a fixed price. But anything produced beyond the quota could be sold at the market price, which was usually higher. So producers had a strong reason to produce more, and over time markets handled a growing share of trade.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the incentive in dual pricing
slides.body_md: An imagined factory produces 1,400 tonnes. The quota is 1,000 tonnes at a fixed price of 20; the rest sells at the market price of 30 (price units a tonne).
bullets: Step 1 — Quota revenue: 1,000 × 20 = **20,000**.
Step 2 — Extra output: 400 × 30 = **12,000**.
Step 3 — Total: **32,000**, against 28,000 if everything sold at the fixed price.
Step 4 — The gain of **4,000** rewards producing beyond the quota.

slides.narration: Let us put numbers on the idea. The factory sells its quota of one thousand tonnes at the fixed price and earns twenty thousand. The extra four hundred tonnes sell at the market price and earn twelve thousand more. If everything had been sold at the fixed price, it would earn only twenty eight thousand. The difference of four thousand is the reward for producing more.

slides.body_md: A quota sold to the state at fixed prices, and extra output sold at market prices. What is this called?
slides.narration: You have just worked through an example of this arrangement. Name it.

slides.heading: Township enterprises, SEZs and foreign investment
slides.body_md: **Township and village enterprises**, owned by local collectives, grew fast and competed with state firms.

nodes.label: Special economic zones on the coast

visual.alt: Flow of how special economic zones worked: better infrastructure and freer rules attract foreign direct investment, factories produce for export, bringing jobs, technology and foreign exchange
visual.caption: How SEZs helped

slides.narration: Two more reforms changed Chinese industry. Township and village enterprises, owned and run by local collectives, grew quickly and gave state owned firms real competition. And special economic zones offered good infrastructure and freer rules to foreign investors. Follow the flow: investment arrived, factories produced for export, and the country gained jobs, technology and foreign exchange.

slides.heading: Sex ratio and density: reading the measures
bullets: **Sex ratio** = number of females per 1,000 males; a **low** sex ratio means fewer females.
**Density** = population ÷ area, in persons per square kilometre.
A low sex ratio often reflects a **preference for sons**; strict limits on family size can worsen it.
slides.narration: Two measures appear again and again in comparison questions. The sex ratio counts females for every thousand males, so a low number means fewer females. Density is population divided by area. When families are allowed very few children, a preference for sons can push the sex ratio down further, which is a social as well as an economic concern.

slides.heading: What the indices leave out
bullets: Human development indices measure **health, education and income**.
They do **not** measure **liberty**: political and civil freedoms, protection of rights.
Some economists suggest adding **liberty indicators** for a fuller picture.
slides.narration: Human development indices are useful, but they are not the whole story. They measure health, education and income. They say nothing about how free people are to take part in decisions or how well their rights are protected. Some economists therefore suggest adding liberty indicators. In an answer, mentioning this limit shows balanced judgement.

slides.body_md: True or false? Life expectancy and literacy also measure political freedom.

Step 3 — Number the points; one point earns about one mark.

slides.narration: Let us weigh the paths fairly. China achieved rapid growth on a strong base of health and education, but now faces ageing and a low sex ratio. India has grown steadily, led by services, though many workers are still in farming. Pakistan raised food output and services, but relied heavily on remittances and aid, so its growth was uneven. Compare them on growth, population, sectors and human development, and remember the limits of each measure.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 2
bullets: Never quote current GDP, HDI ranks or population numbers from memory; state the **broad order** (China ahead on most).
Link **household plots** and **dual pricing** to **incentives**: that is the reason output rose.
One-child policy: write both effects, **ageing** and a **lower sex ratio**.
In comparison answers, mention **both countries in every point**.
For evaluation questions, add a limit: indices leave out **liberty**.
Data case: compute per capita growth as GDP growth minus population growth, and show the subtraction.
slides.narration: Final tips. Do not invent exact figures; describe the broad order. When you explain why China's output rose, connect each reform to incentives. For the one child policy, give both ageing and the sex ratio. In every comparison point, name both countries. And in evaluation questions, a short line on what the indices leave out earns credit for balance.

sections.body_md:
Comparing **neighbours** is fair because they share history, geography and similar problems. Around **1950** India, Pakistan and China were all **poor, mainly agricultural** economies with low incomes.

- **First five-year plans announced:** India **1951**, China **1953**, Pakistan **1956**.
- **Major reforms began:** China **1978**, Pakistan **1988**, India **1991**.

Countries in the region also cooperate through groupings such as **SAARC** (set up in 1985).

sections.heading: 2. Pakistan's development path
sections.body_md:
- **Mixed economy** after 1947, with planning (first plan announced 1956).
- **Late 1950s–1960s:** **import substitution**: consumer-goods industries behind **tariff protection**.
- **1960s:** the **Green Revolution** raised food-grain output; farming was **mechanised** and the state invested in infrastructure in some regions.
- **1970s:** **nationalisation of capital goods industries**.
- **Late 1970s–1980s:** **denationalisation** and encouragement to the private sector, supported by financial help from Western countries and **remittances** from emigrant workers, many in **West Asia**.
- **1988:** economic **reforms** began after a financial crisis.

**Why growth was uneven:** farm output depended on the **weather**; foreign exchange came largely from **remittances and foreign aid**, not from a growing base of manufactured exports; and **political instability** made long-term policy difficult. In both India and Pakistan, **services** became the largest sector of output.

sections.heading: 3. China before 1978
sections.body_md:
- **1949:** People's Republic set up; important sectors brought under **state direction**; **first plan 1953**.
- **Great Leap Forward (1958):** a campaign to **industrialise on a massive scale**; people set up **backyard industries** (for example small steel furnaces); in rural areas **communes** farmed land **collectively**.
- **Setbacks:** a **severe famine**, linked to drought and to the campaign's own policies, in which a very large number of people died; a conflict with the Soviet Union led to the **withdrawal of Soviet experts**.
- **Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966–76):** students and professionals were sent to **work and learn in the countryside**.

Even so, the pre-reform years spread **basic education and health care** widely and built some rural infrastructure, a base that helped later growth.

sections.heading: 4. China's reforms from 1978
sections.body_md:
Reforms came **in phases**. The **first phase** covered **agriculture, foreign trade and investment**; the **later phase** covered industry.

- **Agriculture:** commune land divided into **plots for households**; each family paid the taxes fixed by the government and **kept the rest**, so effort was rewarded.
- **Industry:** private firms and **township and village enterprises** (owned by local collectives) were allowed to **compete** with **state-owned enterprises**, pushing all of them to be efficient.
- **Dual pricing:** a **quota** sold to the state at fixed prices, anything above it at **market prices**.
- **Special economic zones:** coastal areas with good facilities and freer rules to attract **foreign direct investment** and promote exports.

The result was rapid, **manufacturing-led** growth.

sections.heading: 5. Comparing population and the structure of output
sections.body_md:
**Population (broad patterns):**
- China introduced the **one-child policy** in the late **1970s** (from about 1979). Population growth slowed sharply; after a few decades the **share of elderly people rose** (**ageing**) and the policy was later relaxed.
- The **sex ratio** (females per 1,000 males) is **low and biased against females** in all three countries; son preference is one cause.
- India and Pakistan have **younger** populations that still grow faster than China's.

**Output and sectors:**
- **China:** growth led mainly by **manufacturing**; a large, fast movement of workers **out of agriculture**.
- **India and Pakistan:** **services** are the largest and fastest-growing sector of output, while **agriculture still employs a large share** of workers.

**Useful calculations:** growth rate = change ÷ original × 100; per capita income growth ≈ GDP growth − population growth; density = population ÷ area; sex ratio = females ÷ males × 1,000.

sections.heading: 6. Human development and appraisal
sections.body_md:
- On **most human development indicators** (life expectancy, literacy, income per head), **China is ahead** of India and Pakistan; India and Pakistan are **close to each other**, each ahead on some indicators.
- A main reason for China's lead is its early spread of **health care and primary education**.
- **Limits:** these indices do not measure **liberty** (political and civil freedoms, protection of rights) or how fairly gains are shared; some economists suggest **liberty indicators**.

**Appraisal:** China achieved the fastest growth but faces ageing and a low sex ratio; India grew steadily, led by services, with many workers still in farming; Pakistan raised food output and services but depended on remittances, aid and the weather. **Lessons:** invest in people, link reward to effort, build a broad export base, keep policy stable.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up the reform years: **China 1978, Pakistan 1988, India 1991**.
- Saying Pakistan privatised in the 1970s: it **nationalised** capital goods industries then.
- Quoting exact current GDP, HDI ranks or population figures: describe the **broad order** instead.
- Writing a comparison that describes one country only: name **both countries in every point**.
- Saying a low sex ratio means more females: it means **fewer females** per 1,000 males.
- Forgetting that per capita growth ≈ GDP growth − population growth.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: correct option or value.
- 3 marks: three distinct points (about 50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five numbered points (about 80–120 words); comparisons give both countries per point; evaluations end with a balanced judgement.
- Case-based: use the figures in the table or passage, and show each step of a calculation.

questions.stem_md: India and Pakistan became independent nations in 1947. In which year was the People's Republic of China established?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1949. The People's Republic of China was established in 1949, two years after India and Pakistan gained independence; 1951 is the start of India's First Five Year Plan and 1978 the start of China's reforms.

questions.stem_md: All three neighbours began planned development within a few years of each other. Which order of the announcement of their first five-year plans is correct?

options.text_md: China (1951), India (1953), Pakistan (1956)
Pakistan (1951), India (1953), China (1956)
India (1951), Pakistan (1953), China (1956)
India (1951), China (1953), Pakistan (1956)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** India (1951), China (1953), Pakistan (1956). India announced its first plan in 1951, China in 1953 and Pakistan in 1956 (Pakistan's first plan is often called the Medium Term Development Plan).

questions.stem_md: Around 1950, which feature was shared by the economies of India, Pakistan and China?

options.text_md: A large share of the workforce depended on agriculture and incomes were low
Services produced most of national output
Most people lived in large cities
All three had already completed land reforms and industrialisation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A large share of the workforce depended on agriculture and incomes were low. All three began as poor, mainly agricultural economies with low incomes. A services-led output, urban majorities and completed industrialisation came much later, if at all.

questions.stem_md: Like India, Pakistan chose a **mixed economy** after independence. What does this mean for the way its economy was organised?

options.text_md: The state owned every farm and factory
The government played no part in economic decisions
Both the public sector and the private sector had a role in production
Foreign companies ran all major industries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both the public sector and the private sector had a role in production. In a mixed economy the public and private sectors co-exist. Full state ownership describes a command economy, and no role for the state describes a free-market economy.

questions.stem_md: Which policy change marked Pakistan's economy in the 1970s?

options.text_md: The Great Leap Forward
Creation of people's communes
Nationalisation of capital goods industries
Withdrawal of high-value notes as legal tender

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Nationalisation of capital goods industries. In the 1970s Pakistan nationalised capital goods industries. The Great Leap Forward and communes belong to China's history, and note withdrawal is unrelated.

questions.stem_md: Pakistan, facing a financial crisis, began economic reforms in which year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1988. Pakistan initiated reforms in 1988. China began in 1978 and India in 1991.

questions.stem_md: An economist studying Pakistan's growth notes that, in many years, foreign exchange came largely from abroad rather than from a steady rise in exports of manufactured goods. Which two sources is she most likely to point to?

options.text_md: Profits of state-run communes and township enterprises
Earnings from special economic zones set up in 1978
Tourist spending and sales of IT services to the USA
Remittances from Pakistani workers abroad (notably in West Asia) and loans and grants from other countries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Remittances from Pakistani workers abroad (notably in West Asia) and loans and grants from other countries. Pakistan relied heavily on remittances from emigrants (many in West Asia) and on foreign loans and aid. Communes, township enterprises and 1978 SEZs describe China.

questions.stem_md: In both India and Pakistan, the Green Revolution of the 1960s raised the output of food grains. Which further change did it bring in Pakistan, according to the usual account?

options.text_md: An end to the use of chemical fertilisers
Mechanisation of farming and more public investment in infrastructure in some areas
Collective farming in communes
A ban on private trade in grain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Mechanisation of farming and more public investment in infrastructure in some areas. The Green Revolution led to mechanisation and greater public investment in infrastructure in selected areas. It increased (not ended) fertiliser use, and communes belong to China.

questions.stem_md: Which explanation is commonly given for why Pakistan's growth rate slowed and was hard to sustain from the late 1980s?

options.text_md: Dependence on agriculture affected by weather, on remittances and on foreign aid, together with political instability
Too rapid a rise in manufactured exports
A one-child policy that shrank its workforce
A complete shift of workers from agriculture to services

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Dependence on agriculture affected by weather, on remittances and on foreign aid, together with political instability. Growth depended on good harvests, remittances and foreign assistance, all uncertain, and on stable policy, which was often lacking. A one-child policy was China's, and Pakistan's export base remained narrow.

questions.stem_md: Compare how the structure of output changed in India and in Pakistan. Which sector became the largest contributor to GDP in both countries?

options.text_md: The primary sector
The tertiary (service) sector
The secondary sector
The household sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The tertiary (service) sector. In both India and Pakistan the service sector became the largest contributor to GDP, even though agriculture still employs a large share of workers.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fall in the number of workers going abroad can hurt Pakistan's balance of payments.

**Reason (R):** Remittances sent home by emigrant workers have been an important source of foreign exchange for Pakistan.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: fewer emigrants means fewer remittances, so less foreign exchange comes in.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** India and Pakistan both followed a mixed economy with a public sector in the early decades.

**Reason (R):** Pakistan began economic reforms in 1988, a few years before India.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R (the date of Pakistan's reforms) does not explain why both countries chose a mixed economy in the early decades.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the 1970s Pakistan moved away from the public sector and privatised all its capital goods industries.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** In the 1970s Pakistan did the opposite: it nationalised capital goods industries. The shift towards denationalisation and the private sector came later, from the late 1970s and 1980s.

questions.stem_md: The real GDP of an imagined country rose from ₹1,250 thousand crore to ₹1,325 thousand crore in one year. What was its growth rate (in per cent)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Increase = 1,325 − 1,250 = 75.
Step 2: Growth rate = 75 ÷ 1,250 × 100 = 6 per cent.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined South Asian economy, GDP is ₹1,200 thousand crore, of which services produce ₹540 thousand crore. What share of GDP (in per cent) comes from services?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Share = services ÷ GDP × 100.
Step 2: 540 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 45 per cent.

questions.stem_md: An imagined country's GDP grows at 7 per cent a year while its population grows at 2 per cent a year. Approximately how fast (in per cent a year) does its per capita income grow?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Per capita income growth ≈ GDP growth − population growth.
Step 2: 7 − 2 = 5 per cent a year (approximately).

questions.stem_md: Outline two phases in Pakistan's industrial policy between the 1950s and the 1980s.
questions.solution_md: Name each phase with its period and its main policy.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Late 1950s–1960s:** a mixed economy with **import substitution**, building consumer-goods industries behind **tariff protection**.
2. **1970s:** **nationalisation of capital goods industries**; from the late 1970s and 1980s, a shift towards **denationalisation** and encouragement of the **private sector**.

marking_scheme.step: Nationalisation and the later shift to the private sector

questions.stem_md: State two effects of the Green Revolution on Pakistan's agriculture.
questions.solution_md: One effect on output, one on methods or investment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It raised the **output of food grains**, especially wheat, through high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation.
2. It brought **mechanisation** of farming and greater **public investment in infrastructure** such as canals and roads in some regions.

marking_scheme.step: Mechanisation or public investment in infrastructure

questions.stem_md: Why is growth that depends on remittances and foreign aid considered less secure than growth based on rising exports of manufactured goods? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: One point on uncertainty of the source, one on productive capacity.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Remittances and aid depend on **conditions abroad** (jobs in other countries, donors' decisions), which the home country cannot control.
2. They do not build the country's own **productive capacity**; exports of manufactures come from **domestic factories, skills and technology** that keep growing.

marking_scheme.step: Does not build domestic productive capacity

questions.stem_md: Compare the development paths of India and Pakistan on any three points.
questions.solution_md: Three points, each saying how the two countries are alike or different.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Strategy:** both chose a **mixed economy** with five-year plans and import substitution in the early decades.
2. **Reforms:** Pakistan began reforms in **1988**, India in **1991**, both after financial stress.
3. **Sources of growth:** in both, **services** became the largest sector of output; Pakistan has depended more on **remittances and foreign aid**, and its growth has been more uneven, partly because of **political instability**.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons commonly offered for the slowdown of Pakistan's economy after the late 1980s.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct reasons: farm dependence, external sources of funds, instability.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Agriculture**, still a large source of income, depended on **weather and good harvests**, so output swung from year to year.
2. Foreign exchange came largely from **remittances and foreign aid** rather than from growing **manufactured exports**.
3. **Political instability** and frequent changes in policy discouraged long-term investment.

questions.stem_md: Describe the main stages of Pakistan's development strategy from independence to the reforms of 1988, and explain one strength and one weakness of the path it followed.
questions.solution_md: Four stages in order, then a strength and a weakness.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Mixed economy:** after 1947 Pakistan gave roles to both the **public and private sectors**, with five-year plans from **1956**.
2. **Import substitution (late 1950s–1960s):** consumer-goods industries grew behind **tariff protection**; the **Green Revolution** raised grain output and brought mechanisation.
3. **1970s:** **capital goods industries were nationalised**.
4. **Late 1970s–1980s:** a turn to **denationalisation** and the private sector, supported by Western aid and **remittances** from workers in West Asia; **reforms began in 1988**.
5. **Appraisal:** a **strength** was higher food output and a growing service sector; a **weakness** was reliance on **remittances, aid and farm output**, with **political instability** making growth uneven.

marking_scheme.step: Shift to the private sector and 1988 reforms

questions.stem_md: The Great Leap Forward campaign, launched in China in 1958, aimed mainly at

options.text_md: opening the country to foreign investment
reducing the role of the state in farming
industrialising the country on a massive scale
limiting each family to one child

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** industrialising the country on a massive scale. The Great Leap Forward (1958) aimed at rapid, large-scale industrialisation, including small industries set up in villages. Foreign investment came with the 1978 reforms, and the one-child policy from about 1979.

questions.stem_md: During the Great Leap Forward, people were encouraged to set up industries in their backyards. What was the intention?

options.text_md: To export toys and electronics to Europe
To replace farming completely with services
To reduce the number of people employed
To spread industrial production, such as making steel, to villages across the country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To spread industrial production, such as making steel, to villages across the country. Backyard furnaces were meant to spread industry, especially steel-making, into rural areas and speed up industrialisation.

questions.stem_md: Under China's commune system in rural areas, how was land farmed?

options.text_md: Each family owned and farmed its own plot for profit
Foreign companies leased the land
Land was left fallow to restore fertility
People cultivated land collectively

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** People cultivated land collectively. In the communes, people cultivated land collectively. Household plots for each family came with the reforms after 1978.

questions.stem_md: The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution in China took place during
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1966–76. The Cultural Revolution ran from 1966 to 1976; during it, students and professionals were sent to work and learn in the countryside. Reforms began in 1978.

questions.stem_md: When China began its reforms in 1978, in which areas were they introduced first?

options.text_md: Defence and space research
Agriculture, foreign trade and investment
Banking only
Population control only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Agriculture, foreign trade and investment. The reforms were introduced in phases: the first phase covered agriculture, foreign trade and investment; reforms in industry and other areas followed.

questions.stem_md: After 1978 a farming family in rural China was allotted a plot of commune land. After paying the taxes fixed by the government, it could keep its income. Which reform does this describe?

options.text_md: The division of commune land into plots for individual households (the household responsibility idea)
The Great Leap Forward
The creation of special economic zones
The Cultural Revolution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The division of commune land into plots for individual households (the household responsibility idea). questions.stem_md: Comparing the composition of output, which statement about China and India is generally accepted?

questions.stem_md: Describe any three reforms introduced in China from 1978.
questions.solution_md: Three reforms from different areas: agriculture, industry and pricing, foreign investment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Agriculture:** commune land was divided into **plots for households**, which kept the income left after paying fixed taxes.
2. **Industry:** private firms and **township and village enterprises** were allowed to compete with **state-owned enterprises**; **dual pricing** let firms sell output above a quota at market prices.
3. **Opening up:** **special economic zones** were created to attract **foreign direct investment** and promote exports.

marking_scheme.step: Competition and dual pricing in industry

questions.stem_md: Many economists argue that China's reforms after 1978 succeeded partly because of what it had built earlier. Explain this argument with three points.
questions.solution_md: Three foundations from the pre-reform period and how reforms built on them.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Before 1978 China had expanded **basic education and health care**, so it had a **healthier, more literate workforce** ready for factory work.
2. **Land reforms and communes** had built rural **infrastructure** such as irrigation and roads, which supported higher farm output once incentives improved.
3. Earlier efforts gave it an **industrial base**; reforms then added **incentives, competition and foreign investment** to use these foundations more efficiently.

questions.stem_md: Compare the change in the sectoral structure of output and employment in China and India since the reforms.
questions.solution_md: One point on China, one on India, one comparing employment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In **China**, **manufacturing (industry)** became the main driver of growth, and a large share of workers **moved out of agriculture** into factories.
2. In **India**, the **service sector** has led the growth of output, while industry's share grew more slowly.
3. In India **agriculture still employs a large share of workers** although its share of output is small, so many workers remain in low-productivity farming.

marking_scheme.step: India: agriculture still a large employer

questions.stem_md: Compare the approach of the Great Leap Forward with the approach of China's reforms after 1978. Which do you consider more effective, and why?
questions.solution_md: Describe both approaches and give a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Great Leap Forward** relied on **mass campaigns and collective production** (communes, backyard industries) directed by the state.
2. The **reforms** relied on **incentives and markets**: household plots, dual pricing, competition and foreign investment.
3. The **reforms were more effective**, because they linked **reward to effort** and brought capital and technology, producing sustained growth, while the earlier campaign suffered sharp setbacks.

questions.stem_md: Trace China's development path from 1949 to the reforms of 1978 and after, explaining how its strategy changed.
questions.solution_md: Five stages in order, showing the shift from campaigns and collectives to incentives and markets.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **1949–53:** the People's Republic was set up in **1949**; the economy was state-directed, and the **first five-year plan began in 1953**.
2. **Great Leap Forward (1958):** a campaign of mass **industrialisation**, with backyard industries and **communes** for collective farming; a severe famine and the withdrawal of Soviet experts caused serious setbacks.
3. **Cultural Revolution (1966–76):** students and professionals were sent to work in the **countryside**.
4. **Reforms from 1978:** in phases — **household plots** in agriculture, then industry; **township and village enterprises** and private firms competed with state enterprises; **dual pricing**.
5. **Opening up:** **special economic zones** attracted **FDI**, and manufacturing exports drove rapid growth.

questions.stem_md: India, Pakistan and China started their journeys at about the same time with similar problems. Compare their development experience on growth, population and human development, and draw a balanced conclusion.
questions.solution_md: Compare on each dimension, then give a balanced conclusion that notes the limits of the comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Starting point:** all three were **poor, mainly agricultural** economies around **1947–49**, and began five-year plans in the 1950s.
2. **Growth:** **China** grew fastest after **1978**, led by **manufacturing** and exports; **India** grew steadily, led more by **services**; **Pakistan**'s growth was more **uneven**, relying on remittances and aid.
3. **Population:** China's **one-child policy** slowed population growth, but brought **ageing** and a lower sex ratio; India and Pakistan still have younger, faster-growing populations.
4. **Human development:** China is **ahead on most indicators**; India and Pakistan are closer to each other.
5. **Conclusion:** each path had costs and gains; human development measures leave out **liberty**, so growth figures alone do not settle which path is best.

questions.stem_md: Explain why China has done better than India and Pakistan on most human development indicators, and why such indicators do not tell the whole story.
questions.solution_md: Reasons for China's lead, the position of the other two, then the limits of the measures.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Early social investment:** even before 1978, China spread **basic health care** and **primary education** widely, including in rural areas.
2. **Effects:** this raised **life expectancy** and **literacy**, and lowered infant deaths.
3. **Growth:** rapid growth after 1978 raised **income per head**, which also counts in human development measures.
4. **India and Pakistan** spread education and health more slowly, so they lag on several indicators, though each does better on some.
5. **Limits:** these indicators leave out **liberty** — political and civil freedoms and protection of rights — and say little about how fairly gains are shared, so they give only part of the picture.

marking_scheme.step: Effect on life expectancy and literacy

questions.stem_md: What lessons can a developing country draw from the experiences of India, Pakistan and China? Give five points.
questions.solution_md: Five lessons, each tied to the experience of at least one of the three countries.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Invest in people early:** China's spread of **health and education** prepared a workforce for later growth.
2. **Incentives matter:** output rose when farmers and firms could **keep the rewards** of extra effort, as with household plots.
3. **Build a broad export base:** growth that relies on **remittances and aid**, as Pakistan's often did, is less secure than growth from **manufactured exports**.
4. **Stability and continuity** of policy encourage long-term investment.
5. **Balance growth with other goals:** population policies affect **ageing and the sex ratio**, and growth figures do not measure **freedoms**, so a country should weigh these too.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined countries have the same area. Country P has twice the population of Country Q. How do their densities of population compare?

options.text_md: Q's density is twice P's
P's density is twice Q's
Both have the same density
P's density is four times Q's

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** P's density is twice Q's. Density = population ÷ area. With equal areas, twice the population means twice the density.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined countries both grow at 6 per cent a year. Population grows at 1 per cent in Country X and at 3 per cent in Country Y. What follows?

options.text_md: Per capita income rises equally fast in both
Per capita income rises faster in Y because it has more people
Per capita income rises faster in X (about 5 per cent) than in Y (about 3 per cent)
Per capita income falls in Y

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Per capita income rises faster in X (about 5 per cent) than in Y (about 3 per cent). Per capita growth ≈ GDP growth − population growth: about 5 per cent in X and 3 per cent in Y. It still rises in Y, only more slowly.

questions.stem_md: Using the rule of 70, a population growing at 2 per cent a year will double in roughly how many years?

options.text_md: 20 years
70 years
140 years
35 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 35 years. Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate = 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Human development indicators such as life expectancy and literacy also measure how much political freedom people enjoy.

questions.solution_md: **False.** They do not. Life expectancy, literacy and income say nothing directly about political and civil freedoms, which is why some economists suggest adding liberty indicators.
